passage: I'm Sachin, and I sit behind Amandeep in our Year 10 form group in Leicester. I started keeping count after the careers fair. A visitor at the engineering stall shook his hand and asked, "And where are you really from?" Amandeep said, "Here. Born at the hospital down the road." The man laughed and waited, as if a better answer was coming. On Tuesday the new drama teacher told him his English was "lovely, so clear". He has never spoken anything else at school. On Thursday a supply teacher handed back his chemistry test, looked at the mark, then at him, and said, "Well! Didn't expect that." Each time, Amandeep smiled and gave a small nod. But on Friday, when our group was planning where to go after exams, he said, "Somewhere nobody asks where I'm from." Nobody laughed. I can't say what he felt exactly. I know he has stopped putting his hand up.

qa.q: Where was Amandeep first asked where he was really from?
qa.a: At the engineering stall at the careers fair.

qa.q: What does Amandeep's line about going "somewhere nobody asks where I'm from" suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests the small comments had piled up until he felt like an outsider in the town he was born in; Sachin noticed it didn't sound like a joke.

qa.q: After Friday, what choice does Sachin face, and what could make a difference?
qa.a: Sachin can keep counting silently or act on it, for example by checking in with Amandeep privately and, next time someone presses, backing up the first answer: "He said here."

qa.q: How might the visitor at the stall have seen the question, compared with how it landed?
qa.a: The visitor probably thought it was friendly curiosity, but by laughing and waiting for a 'better' answer, the man treated Amandeep's real home as not good enough.

grounding: A teenager born in the city is asked where he is really from, praised for his English and called surprisingly clever, and the small remarks add up to feeling like an outsider.

subtopic: Microaggressions (respectful, balanced treatment)
passage:
Monday, first week. Jaya had joined the private school in Class 11 on a scholarship. In the physics lab a boy leaned over her neat circuit and said, "Wow. Smart for a scholarship kid." Jaya laughed along. Her lab partner, Mehak, frowned but said nothing.
Two weeks later. The class teacher handed back the essays and smiled at Jaya. "Your English is really good, considering." Considering what, Jaya wanted to ask. At lunch a girl asked how she "managed" such marks "coming from there". Each thing was tiny. Jaya began eating her rotis in the library.
A month later. Mehak found her between the shelves. "You've stopped sitting with us." Jaya shrugged, then it came out. "Every day someone reminds me I'm the one who doesn't fit. Nobody means it. It's just every day." Mehak sat on the floor beside her and opened her tiffin. "Then tell me the next one when it happens. I'm listening."

qa.q: Where did Jaya start eating lunch?
qa.a: In the library, between the shelves.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when she said, "Nobody means it. It's just every day"?
qa.a: She felt worn down and singled out; no single comment was big, but the steady repetition made her feel she didn't belong at the new school.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the third beat, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Mehak came looking for Jaya and asked why she had stopped sitting with them, which let Jaya say the pattern out loud instead of carrying it alone.

qa.q: How might the class teacher have meant "really good, considering", and how did it land for Jaya?
qa.a: The teacher probably meant it as warm praise, but for Jaya the word 'considering' was one more sign that people expected less of her.

grounding: A scholarship student hears one small remark after another about being clever or well-spoken for her background, and over weeks they add up to feeling like an outsider.

Sahil,
I tried to say this at the bus stop and it came out wrong, so I'm writing it.
At the science fair, when the judges praised your bridge, I said really loudly, "Obviously! It's in his blood. His family runs the cycle shop, he was born to fix things." I meant it as the biggest compliment. I was proud of you.
Then you didn't talk the whole ride home, and Tanya told me later what you'd said to her: that you spent three weeks on the load calculations, and I made it sound like your hands did it and your head didn't.
Honestly, I didn't see it. I was shocked. I kept thinking, but I was being nice!
Being nice and landing nice aren't the same thing, I get that now. The calculations were yours. I'm sorry I made it about the shop.
Hemant

qa.a: Hemant could have praised the actual work, something like "Sahil did all the load calculations", instead of tying the bridge to the family's cycle shop.

qa.a: To Sahil, three weeks of careful maths was turned into an inherited knack, as if the family shop mattered more than Sahil's own mind 😔

passage: Okay, Rukmini, you asked what I learnt this term, so here's the embarrassing one. I'm Gargi, and I'm the joker in our group, right? Everyone knows me for it. During the group project, Francis kept the only calculator on his desk, and I said, "Classic only child, never learnt to share," and did a little spoilt-baby voice. Everybody laughed. Francis laughed too, sort of. I thought that was the end of it. Two days later his friend told me Francis went home upset. Apparently he's heard that line since forever, and he's the one who photocopies his notes for half the class. I was honestly shocked. I kept saying, "But it was a joke! I like him!" And I do. That's the weird part. I meant it as teasing between friends, and it still landed as one more person calling him selfish. I said sorry the next morning, with no jokes attached.

qa.a: Gargi was genuinely shocked and a bit defensive, because the joke came from affection and Gargi never imagined it could feel like an insult.

qa.a: Gargi apologised the next morning with no jokes attached, which took the hurt seriously instead of explaining the good intent again.

qa.a: Francis has heard it forever, so even from a friend it feels like one more person calling him selfish, despite sharing notes with half the class.

subtopic: Microaggressions (respectful, balanced treatment)
passage: On the third day of his placement on a hospital ward in Leeds, Gabriel was changing a dressing when Nadia, his mentor, breezed past and told the patient, "Don't mind him, he's our male nurse. Couldn't get into medicine, bless him." The patient chuckled. Gabriel kept his hands steady. It wasn't true; nursing had been his first choice since he'd sat by his grandfather's bed at fourteen. On the bus home he turned it over and over. Was he being touchy? She'd said it with a smile. If he raised it, she'd be signing off his competencies next week. If he didn't, he'd hear it again, and again he'd smile. He typed her a message, deleted it, typed a shorter one. His thumb hovered. Then he slid the phone into his pocket, too tired to decide tonight, and rested his forehead against the cold window.

qa.q: What did Nadia tell the patient about Gabriel?
qa.a: "Don't mind him, he's our male nurse. Couldn't get into medicine, bless him."

qa.q: What was Gabriel worried about as he weighed whether to speak up?
qa.a: He wondered if he was being touchy, and he worried that raising it with his mentor could cost him, since she would be signing off his competencies next week.

qa.q: With his thumb over the message, what choices did Gabriel have, and what would each cost?
qa.a: He could send a short, calm message or ask for a quiet word, risking friction; or let it go for now, which avoids conflict but may mean carrying the same remark again. Either is a fair choice.

qa.q: How might Nadia see things if Gabriel never mentions it?
qa.a: Nadia would likely think it was harmless teasing and keep repeating it, never knowing it followed Gabriel all the way home on the bus.

grounding: A nursing student hears a demeaning remark from his mentor and weighs whether speaking up is worth the friction, while silence is already wearing on him.

passage: The placement cell smelt of toner and old files. Hansa handed over her form for the core mechanical drive, and the officer, not unkindly, slid a second sheet across. Four years of lathe work, a gold in the design project. Was she overreacting to one tired man's habit? He signed the shortlists, and twenty people were in the queue. Staying quiet would be easy; she'd been doing it since first year, and it was getting heavy. She pushed the HR sheet back, gently. "Only mechanical, sir. That's the job I want." passage: Pema, you asked how I survived my first posting, so here is one small thing. I was twenty-four, the only woman officer at a bank branch in a mill town, and the senior manager, Mr Bhosle, was a decent man. But whenever a client came in, he'd say, "Meet our lady officer. Only here till her marriage, ha!" I laughed the first week. By the fourth, clients were walking past my desk to wait for him. So one evening, after we'd locked the cash, I asked, "Sir, when you say that, what do you mean by it?" He blinked. "Only that in my day, girls left." I said, "I know you mean it kindly. Here is how it comes across: clients think I'm temporary, so they don't trust my files." He was quiet a long time. Next morning he introduced me as "Officer Arohi, handles our loans." We stayed friends till he retired.

passage:
Warden's note, college mess, Thursday.
At dinner a final-year student at the next table kept commenting on Zeenat's kurta and telling her to "turn around, let's see". Several people looked away. Chinmay, from her lab batch, stood up, and I expected shouting. There was none. He walked Zeenat to the water cooler and, from where I stood, I heard him ask, "Do you want me to say something, report it, or just sit with you?" She said, "Just sit. I'll decide later." He sat with her until she finished eating and did not look at the other table once.
Friday morning, Zeenat came to my office, with Chinmay waiting outside. She wanted to file a complaint. passage:

Week three. The audit came back. Ayesha's own product pages had two hundred images with no descriptions. Fixing them meant her weekend. She told Leela she was "swamped", muted the accessibility thread, and changed the subject whenever it came up at lunch.
Week five. Leela stopped by her desk. "You were the loudest in week one. I haven't heard from you since the actual work started." Ayesha felt her face burn and nearly said, "I've been busy." Instead she said, "You're right. Which pages first?" Leela pulled up a chair and let her hear how the screen reader stumbled over each blank image.

qa.q: How many images on Ayesha's pages had no descriptions?
qa.a: Two hundred images.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling after the first post, and what does it suggest about the motive?
qa.a: She felt warm all afternoon over the forty reactions, which suggests the support was partly about being seen as good.

qa.q: What choice at Leela's desk marked Ayesha's turning point?
qa.a: Instead of saying "I've been busy", Ayesha admitted Leela was right and asked which pages to fix first, accepting the correction and staying with the uncomfortable work.

qa.q: What might the silence between week one and week five have been like for Leela?
qa.a: Leela watched loud cheering turn into a muted thread the moment effort was needed, which likely felt like being a talking point rather than being supported.

grounding: A young professional loudly backs a colleague's accessibility request for applause, drops it when it costs her weekend, then accepts correction and starts the work.

passage: Kiran, before you post that, sit with your old aunt a minute. When I was twenty-five I worked in the accounts office of a cotton mill. The women spinners wanted a crèche; their babies slept on sacks beside the looms. I made a speech at the gate. A reporter took my photo, and my mother cut it out and framed it. I was very pleased with Ankita the brave. Then the manager hinted my promotion might "take longer". And the spinners asked me to come on Sundays to help list the children's names. Suddenly I was always busy. One day Kamala-bai stopped me in the yard. "You spoke for us once," she said. "Come and listen once." It stung for a week. Then I went. I sat on the floor and wrote names for three Sundays. The crèche opened the next year. The photo? I took it down. I kept the list.

qa.a: It shows Ankita cared a lot about looking brave, the photo and the praise, more than about the crèche itself.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Ankita's story, and what choice followed?
qa.a: Kamala-bai's words, "Come and listen once", stung, and after a week Ankita chose to go and spent three Sundays on the floor writing the children's names.

qa.q: How might Kamala-bai have seen Ankita before and after those Sundays?
qa.a: At first Kamala-bai likely saw someone who used the spinners' cause for a photo and then vanished; afterwards, someone who finally listened and did the dull work.
